public_rationale: The searches did not identify a longitudinal record connecting increased discouragement of US children to enthusiasm about AI coding. A pre-forecast survey found broad willingness to encourage coding, but that does not rule out later growth in discouragement. No decisive event meets the early-resolution rule.
limitations: Public attitudes toward coding are not the same as actual advice to children.
The available baseline is not a parent- or educator-specific panel.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Hype about AI coding will increasingly lead people to discourage American children from learning to code.

statement.excerpt: People are increasingly going to discourage American children from learning to code based on naive enthusiasm from people like Roose.
statement.document_title: Decoding (and debunking) Hard Fork’s Kevin Roose

from_speaker: discourage American children from learning to code
based on naive enthusiasm from people like Roose
our_interpretation: The forecast concerns increasing discouragement directed at US children, caused by enthusiasm about AI coding.
The word naive is evaluative and is not separately scored.
Roose is an example of the proposed influence; proof need not identify him personally.
Enrollment changes alone do not establish either discouragement or its cause.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable observations over time show increasing discouragement of American children learning programming and identify enthusiasm about AI coding as a material reason.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable longitudinal evidence finds no increase or a decline in AI-driven discouragement over an agreed assessment period. Because Marcus supplied no endpoint, a temporary contrary trend cannot conclusively refute eventual increase.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Repeated comparable US surveys documenting actual discouragement and its AI-related reasons, with enough causal evidence to distinguish AI enthusiasm from other influences.
